blocks.text: 8.2.2. Applying KISS in Concurrent Programming

A warehouse service moves stock between 100 bins on four threads. A dashboard audit adds up the bins and raises an alert when the total isn't 100,000. The alert fires on almost every audit, yet the closing count is always exactly 100,000. Every bin has its own lock, and every move takes both bins' locks in a fixed order.
Every output is from Java 21 on one 20-core machine; timings come from plain loops, not a benchmark harness.
A Lock per Bin Keeps Every Move Right and Every Total Wrong
No field is read or written without its lock, and the lock order rules out deadlock. Four threads make random moves for one second while a fifth audits in a loop:
lock per bin      11,855,782 moves,    258,239 audits,  247,317 wrong, final total 100,000
Three runs gave 233,571 to 247,366 wrong totals out of 243,962 to 262,097 audits.

Say the audit has added up bins 0 to 40 when a move takes 3 units from bin 70 to bin 12. Bin 12 was counted before the move and bin 70 will be counted after it, so the audit comes out 3 short. A move the other way makes it 3 too high. Each lock protects one bin, and the total is a fact about all 100 at once, which no single lock protects. Inside this design the direct cure is for `total()` to hold all 100 locks, taken in order, for the whole sum.
One Lock Makes the Total Right; One Owner Thread Also Keeps Readers From Waiting

The first fix deletes code: drop the lock array and make `move` and `total` `synchronized`. The second gives the bins an owner: a single-thread executor is the only thread that touches `qty` after construction, so the array needs no lock (unit 5.3.4), and after each move it publishes a copy that nothing changes:
The same race, with the movers waiting on each `Future` and the audit reading `stock().total()`:

owner, snapshot      368,597 moves, 12,285,992 audits,        0 wrong, final total 100,000
one lock           6,952,234 moves,  2,327,678 audits,        0 wrong, final total 100,000

Both are right in all three runs. The volatile write publishes the finished `Stock` (unit 5.2.3), and a reader holds one whole state, from before or after any move, for as long as it likes. `Stock` copies the array. A read-only view of live state would not do: the javadoc of `Collections.unmodifiableMap(m)` says its reads go through to `m`, so it changes under the reader with every move.

The two fixes differ in who waits. With one lock, an audit waits for a move and a move waits for an audit. With an owner, readers never wait: 12 million audits against 2.3 million. Moves cost more: each is a hand-off to another thread and back, and the owner did 340,000 to 490,000 moves a second against the one lock's 6.4 to 9 million. When nobody needs reads that never block, one lock is the simpler choice.

A decision belongs on the owner too. A caller that checks `stock().of(from) >= n` and then submits a move without the check is the check-then-act of unit 5.3.1. Two callers asked to take 3 units from a bin holding 3, while the owner was still busy with an earlier task:

checked on the caller:     first move true, second move true, bin 0 now holds -3
checked inside the task:   first move true, second move false, bin 0 now holds 0

Checked on the caller, both moves read the same snapshot (bin 0 holds 3) and passed. Inside the task, the check runs on the only thread that changes the bins, so nothing comes between it and the move.
A Snapshot of 100,000 Bins Copies 800 KB on Every Move
The same race with 100,000 bins, plus an owner with no snapshot that runs each audit as a task submitted to the owner:

lock per bin      21,433,573 moves,        593 audits,      593 wrong, final total 100,000,000
owner, snapshot       10,542 moves,     28,722 audits,        0 wrong, final total 100,000,000
owner, audit task    137,774 moves,     20,674 audits,        0 wrong, final total 100,000,000
one lock           2,522,335 moves,     28,821 audits,        0 wrong, final total 100,000,000

Every move now copies 800 KB, and the owner managed 10,500 to 12,900 moves a second over three runs. A snapshot suits small state. For large state that changes often, send the read to the owner as a task, which then waits its turn behind the moves, or use one lock (790,000 to 2.5 million moves a second here).

A compareAndSet Loop That Reads the Value Once Spins Forever; incrementAndGet Leaves No Loop to Get Wrong
A counter whose author read that atomics beat locks, with its retry loop written by hand:
Spot the problem before the run. Four threads, a million increments each, two seconds to finish:
hand-written CAS 3 of 4 threads still running after 2 s, count = 1,000,000

Ten runs out of ten ended this way, with the count between 1,000,000 and 1,000,255. `seen` is read once, before the loop. The first time another thread wins, `count` moves past `seen` and never comes back, so every later `compareAndSet(seen, …)` fails: the thread spins at 100 % until the JVM exits. A retry loop has to read the value again on every failure, as `updateAndGet()` does inside the JDK (unit 5.3.2 shows it). `incrementAndGet()` and a `synchronized` method around `count++` leave no loop to write, three runs each:

incrementAndGet  all threads done in 49 ms, count = 4,000,000
synchronized     all threads done in 246 ms, count = 4,000,000
`incrementAndGet()` took 41 to 49 ms and `synchronized` 246 to 294 ms, for four threads doing nothing but counting. For a counter that is the hot spot, unit 5.3.2 measures `LongAdder`.
A Double-Checked Flag Can Say Loaded Before the Value Is; a synchronized Getter Can't
Exchange rates are loaded on first use. The author wanted no lock once they are loaded, and set the flag first so that no second caller starts another load:
The plain version locks every call and uses the value itself as the flag:

Thread A calls `rates()`, and its load is held open while thread B calls `rates()` and for 500 ms after. A second run makes the first load throw. `volatile ref` is the double-checked locking of unit 5.1.3: one `volatile` field holding the map, read once into a local.

In all three runs the flag said "loaded" while the map was still `null`: the flag and the map are two variables. B read the flag without the lock, so it never waited for the load. When the load threw, the flag stayed `true` and the map `null`, and every later call returns `null` until the process restarts. In `SyncRates` there is only the map: `null` means "not loaded", a failed load leaves it `null`, and the next call tries again. The volatile version also has a single variable.

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as thread A
    participant F as FlagRates
    participant B as thread B
    A->>F: rates()
    F->>F: loaded is false, take the lock
    F->>F: loaded = true
    F->>F: rates = loader.get() starts, held open
    B->>F: rates()
    F->>F: loaded is true, skip the lock
    F-->>B: rates, still null
    Note over F: if the load throws, loaded stays true and rates null
The lock costs time. Eight threads that do nothing but call `rates()` 10 million times each:

synchronized  8 threads x 10,000,000 calls: 3,327 ms
volatile ref  8 threads x 10,000,000 calls: 47 ms
Keep the `synchronized` getter until a profile shows it, then switch to the volatile reference.
<!-- practice 3 -->
Summary

items: **A lock per object keeps each object right and leaves every fact about several objects unprotected.** Making the total right inside that design means holding every lock at once.

**One lock fixes it by deleting code; one owner thread with an immutable snapshot fixes it and keeps readers from waiting.** The owner costs a hand-off per write and a copy per snapshot, and decisions about the state are made on the owner, not on a snapshot.
**A hand-written compareAndSet loop that doesn't re-read the value spins forever** after its first lost race. `incrementAndGet()` or `synchronized` is correct with no loop of your own.

**A double-checked flag beside the value can say "loaded" while the value is `null`**, and a failed load leaves it so for good. A `synchronized` getter whose value is its own flag is right; the volatile-reference version of unit 5.1.3 is the fix when the lock shows in a profile.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The warehouse also needs "move 10 units from bin 4 to whichever of bins 7, 8 and 9 has the least stock". Write it for one lock and for the owner thread. Which version needs a new idea?

At what number of bins does the snapshot's copy cost more than the hand-off on your machine? Race four movers against an auditor as this page does, then try a snapshot built from a persistent map instead of a copy.

Your counter must also record the time of the last increment, and readers want both values together. Which of `AtomicLong`, `synchronized` and an immutable pair behind an `AtomicReference` (unit 5.3.2) do you choose, and why?

blocks.text: Design Note: Simple Means Fewer Shared Variables, Not Fewer Lines

Unit 8.2.1 judged simplicity by the code you read. With threads, the measure is how many shared mutable variables a reader has to keep in mind at once, and in how many places they change. `OwnedBins` is longer than `LockedBins`, yet once it is built the only variable two threads share is `stock`, and only the owner writes it. `FlagRates` is longer than `SyncRates` because it keeps a second variable in step with the first, and that second variable is the bug.

The price of that design is throughput: one lock admits one thread at a time and one owner thread does one thing at a time, so neither scales with cores the way the broken per-bin locks did. Unit 8.2.3 counts what the simpler design buys in return: fewer interleavings to reason about and test.
